newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian opposition urges broad government.
newsitem.headline: Albanian opposition urges broad government.

text.p: Albania's main opposition Socialist Party said it had urged President Sali Berisha in talks on Tuesday to agree to a new broad-based government to help end the unrest gripping the south of the country.

Pandeli Majko, one of three Socialist leaders at the talks, said the party had gained "no sense of compromise" from Berisha at the meeting, their first since parliament declared a national state of emergency on Sunday to tackle the crisis.
"We told Berisha we were ready for a wide political accord under which he would stop using the army...and we would agree to form a new broad-based government," Majko told Reuters.
"We are convinced it will be difficult to achieve this but we told Berisha it is no longer a matter of left or right but of protecting people and stopping further blood from being shed.
"We told him that if we reached a common political view then ordinary people who are now on the streets without knowing why would dissociate themselves from the disorder," he said.
"It would then be possible to find the true terrorists" among the protesters, he added.
Asked what was Berisha's response, Majko said the president had told the Socialists, successors to Albania's old communists, "not to try to take power by arms".
"We advised him that we would never want power through blood," Majko said.
Officials in Berisha's ruling Democratic Party, whose leader Tritan Shehu was also at the talks according to Majko, were not immediately available for comment on the meeting.
Berisha has vowed to use the "iron hand" of the law to restore order throughout the country, Europe's poorest nation.
Facing his deepest crisis since coming to office as president in the former Stalinist state in 1992, he has accused communists of orchestrating the anarchy to try to seize power.
Parliament, dominated by the Democratic Party, declared a state of emergency after rioters in the south stormed police and army posts and seized weapons in several towns.
It acted after Berisha failed to stem the disturbances by announcing the resignation of his unpopular prime minister, Aleksander Meksi.
According to a senior Democratic Party source, Berisha had accompanied the concession with an offer to the opposition to call early elections and resign if the Socialists won.
Majko confirmed Berisha had made such an offer at talks last week but said one of the conditions was elections in 45 days.
"It is not possible to hold elections in 45 days... Maybe they could take place some months after a broad-based government has been in office but not in this climate," Majko said.
The Socialists and other forces in the 11-party opposition Forum for Democracy had been pressing before the state of emergency for a technocrat government and early polls.
Security forces have been moving south from Tirana to re-establish authority but the government said armed gangs remain in control of the Adriatic towns of Vlore and Sarande.

Unrest in Albania began two months ago when dubious "get-rich-quick" savings schemes began to collapse, taking the life savings of thousands of Albanians with them. Protests have turned increasingly against Berisha and his ruling party.
The Socialists last year boycotted a general election which they accused Berisha's party of rigging and have not taken up their seats in the chamber, 122 of whose 140 members are Democrats.
